notes.meaning: God introduces His chosen Servant, whom He supports and delights in. The Father places His Holy Spirit on Him so He can bring true justice and God's ways to all nations. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus Christ at His baptism.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek Septuagint translation inserted the names Jacob and Israel into this verse, understanding the Servant here to represent the nation as a whole rather than a coming Messiah.

notes.meaning: The Servant will not shout, quarrel, or try to draw noisy public attention to Himself. Unlike worldly rulers who parade their power, His work is quiet, gentle, and marked by humble confidence.

A bent, cracked reed will not be snapped off, and a flickering lamp wick that is almost out will not be extinguished. This pictures how the Servant treats weak, hurting, and discouraged people with great tenderness rather than crushing them. At the same time, He faithfully establishes true justice without compromise.

The Servant Himself will not grow dim or be crushed by difficulties before His mission is complete. He will persevere until He sets up God's righteous rule on earth. Distant coastlands and nations far away will wait eagerly for His teaching.

The LORD identifies Himself as the Creator who spread out the heavens, formed the earth, and gave breath to every living person. Because God possesses unlimited power over creation, His people can be fully confident that He will fulfill every promise He makes.

God speaks directly to His Servant, promising to take Him by the hand and guard Him. God appoints Him to embody the covenant—a sacred promise binding God and His people together—and to be a light guiding all the nations into truth.

The Servant is sent to give sight to the blind and lead prisoners out of dark dungeons. While this echoes freedom from physical exile, it mainly points to spiritual deliverance from the darkness and trap of sin.

The LORD proclaims His personal name, Yahweh, which marks Him as eternal, self-existing, and completely faithful. He will never share His supreme honor or the praise due to Him with lifeless carved idols.

God reminds His listeners that His past prophecies have already come to pass just as He said. Now He announces brand-new events before they begin to take shape, showing that He controls history from start to finish.

The entire earth is called to sing a brand-new song of praise to the LORD for His coming deliverance. Sailors out on the sea, the oceans themselves, and distant coastlands are all invited to join in celebrating God's grace.

Desert camps, nomadic tribes living in the tents of Kedar, and people living in the high rocky city of Sela are urged to shout for joy. Even the most remote and dry places on earth will rejoice when they hear what God has done.
People everywhere are summoned to give glory to the LORD and spread His praise across far-off islands. The news of God's saving power is meant to be shared freely around the entire globe.

The LORD steps forth like a mighty warrior marching into battle, full of fierce jealousy for His people and His name. He raises a triumphant battle cry to conquer His enemies and end their oppression.

For a long time, God stayed silent and held Himself back while foreign nations ruled over His people. Now, like a mother in labor, He gasps and pants as He brings about a sudden, powerful new deliverance.

God describes His judgment as drying up mountains, vegetation, and flowing rivers. This poetic picture shows that no mighty empire or natural barrier can stop Him when He makes a clear path to free His people.

The LORD promises to lead helpless and confused people along roads they have never known before. He will turn their darkness into bright light, flatten rough roads ahead of them, and never abandon them.

Those who rely on carved images and call metal statues their gods will be turned back in complete shame. God's mighty rescue of His people shows that idols are utterly helpless to protect or save anyone.
God calls out to deaf people to hear and blind people to look up and see. He is speaking of spiritual blindness and deafness, where people have intentionally shut their ears and eyes to His truth.

God asks who could be as blind as His own servant, the nation of Israel, whom He chose to carry His message to the world. Because they had received God's laws and covenants, their refusal to see God's hand was far more tragic than the ignorance of the nations around them.
Israel had witnessed countless miracles and works of God throughout their past, yet they did not take them to heart. Their ears were open to hear the prophets, but they refused to obey what God said.

Because God is righteous and faithful to His own character, He was pleased to make His law great and honorable. He gave Israel His holy instruction so they could reflect His righteousness to the nations.

Instead of walking in honor, the people ended up plundered, trapped in caves, and locked away in enemy prisons. They became easy prey with no human rescuer around to demand that they be sent back home.
The prophet challenges his hearers to pay close attention to this hard reality. He asks who among them will finally listen, learn from their past disasters, and obey God in the future.
Isaiah asks who allowed Jacob to be looted and Israel to be robbed. The answer is the LORD Himself, because the people had sinned against Him and refused to walk in His ways or follow His law.

God poured out the fierce heat of His anger and the destruction of war against His rebellious people like a consuming fire. Yet even while the flames engulfed them, they remained stubborn and refused to take God's correction to heart.
